slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open the lecture by setting the scale. The chapter is not asking whether two spaces look identical under a microscope; it asks whether they have the same navigational geometry from far away. Keep the source span visible so students know this deck is tied to Chapter 05, printed pages 115-164 and PDF pages 126-175.

slides.label: Coarse Agenda
slides.notes: Use this slide as the contract for the session. Every later definition should be heard as a way of ignoring bounded local noise while preserving long-distance measurements. The three rows separate objects, maps, and tests, so students can sort examples instead of memorizing disconnected vocabulary.

slides.label: Word Metrics
slides.notes: Stress that a word metric is a measuring device built from a finite alphabet of moves. The same group can receive different local graph structures from different generating sets. The teaching point is that finite changes can shorten many routes without changing the large-scale type.

slides.label: Same Group, Two Metrics
slides.notes: Read the comparison through the identity map. A diagonal move in the enlarged generating set can compress distance, but only by a bounded linear factor in this sample. The notebook check records the same phenomenon numerically, which turns the picture into evidence for a coarse inequality.

slides.label: Coarse Maps
slides.notes: Pause on the difference between exact and coarse control. A coarse map does not promise to preserve each short distance exactly; it promises that bounded clusters do not explode into unbounded clusters. This is the right language once local subdivision or generator choices are declared irrelevant.

slides.label: Quasi-Isometric Embedding
slides.notes: Make the constants visible. The lower line prevents far apart points from collapsing, while the upper line prevents distances from expanding too quickly. The additive constant allows small-scale exceptions, so students should focus on the linear envelope rather than on exact equality.

slides.label: Quasi-Isometry
slides.notes: An embedding becomes a quasi-isometry only after the target is covered up to bounded error. The visual language is a net: every point of the target lies near the image. This is why an axis in the plane can embed well but still fail to represent the whole plane coarsely.

slides.label: Notebook Distortion Envelope
slides.notes: Connect the lecture deck to the executed notebook. The finite diagnostic is deliberately modest: it samples a radius five window and checks one hundred twenty pairs. The goal is not proof by finite computation, but a concrete inspection target that mirrors the formal inequalities.

slides.label: Quasi-Geodesics
slides.notes: Introduce quasi-geodesics as efficient routes with tolerance. The blue route is exactly geodesic in the grid metric, while the teal route wastes bounded effort but still advances at a linear rate. This idea prepares students for later stability results without assuming such stability in every space.

slides.label: Svarc-Milnor Intuition
slides.notes: Give the theorem as a geometric compression principle. If a finitely generated group acts on a nice large-scale space with finite local complexity and compact quotient, then the orbit map records the space up to quasi-isometry. The tiling picture explains why generators become bounded moves.

slides.label: Orbit Map Roadmap
slides.notes: Do not prove every technical clause on the slide; instead, show how each hypothesis pays for one part of the quasi-isometry. Compact quotient supplies coarse surjectivity, properness prevents infinitely many group elements from living in a bounded region, and the generating set gives Lipschitz control.

slides.label: Distortion
slides.notes: Distortion is where students learn that subgroup inclusion is not automatically a quasi-isometric embedding. The intrinsic metric counts the subgroup's own generators, while the ambient metric may offer shortcuts. Undistorted means these two measuring systems stay linearly comparable.

slides.label: Commutator Shortcuts
slides.notes: Use the commutator square as an intuition pump, not as a new algebra course. In the integer Heisenberg group, central motion can be produced by loops whose side lengths are about the square root of the central exponent. That makes the ambient length much smaller than intrinsic cyclic length.

slides.label: Invariants
slides.notes: Frame invariants as reusable tests. Once a property is known to survive quasi-isometry, it can distinguish groups that no finite change of generators could make equivalent. Some entries are developed in later chapters, so present this slide as a roadmap for the rest of the course.

slides.label: Non-Invariants
slides.notes: This slide prevents a common overreach. Quasi-isometry is powerful because it forgets local details on purpose. Degree, exact angles in a drawing, a preferred presentation, and finite decorations can all change while the large-scale geometry remains the same.

slides.label: Applied Lab
slides.notes: Turn the notebook extension into a short research habit. Students add one generator, predict the effect on the distance envelope, run the experiment, and record a check. The important discipline is to state an invariant before computing, so the visual remains mathematically accountable.

slides.label: Exercise
slides.notes: Let this be a five minute closing task or a homework prompt. The generator vector two comma one gives a new shortcut direction, but because the generating set is still finite, students should expect coarse equivalence with different constants. Ask for inequalities, not just a picture.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by rebuilding the chapter as a chain of implications. Finite generators give word metrics, coarse maps compare those metrics, quasi-isometries identify large-scale geometry, Svarc-Milnor turns good actions into examples, and invariants convert the equivalence relation into a classification tool.
